newsitem.title: USA: Most financial institutions not assessed by FDIC.
newsitem.headline: Most financial institutions not assessed by FDIC.

text.p: Most U.S. banks and savings institutions will pay nothing for federal deposit insurance in the second half of 1997, Federal Deposit Insurance Corp decided on Tuesday.

The agency's board approved a sliding scale of insurance assessments ranging from zero to 27 basis points, with healthy institutions paying less. Since the financial system is in good health, FDIC said, 95 percent of banks and 90 percent of savings institutions would qualify to make no payments.
But savings institutions will have to pay 3.16 basis points to cover interest on Financing Corp, or FICO, bonds.
Banks will have to pay 0.63 basis points for FICO interest.

The federal insurance funds for both banks and savings institutions are projected to remain well capitalized in the second half of the year, FDIC assistant director Fred Carns said at the board meeting.

The bank insurance fund, which totaled $26.85 billion at the end of 1996, is expected to rise to between $27.16 billion to $27.86 billion by year-end, Carns said. Even at the low end, the fund would cover 1.29 percent of insured deposits, above the legally mandated minimum of 1.25 percent.

Based on the health of the industry and interest earnings on the insurance fund, the ratio is more likely to be closer to the high-end projection of 1.42 percent, up from 1.34 percent at the end of 1996, Carns said.

Likewise, the savings industry's insurance fund is expected to rise from $8.89 billion at the end of 1996 to between $9.29 billion and $9.40 billion, Carns said. That would raise the fund's deposit coverage ratio from 1.30 percent at the end of 1996 to between 1.31 percent and 1.43 percent, Carns said.
